title: Using AI check-ins to keep your relationship healthy
summary: Most relationship check-ins die by week three. Why they fail, what makes one survive a busy month, and what an AI read adds to it.
body_markdown:
Most couples who decide to start doing regular check-ins manage about two of them. The first one is genuinely good. The second one is shorter. Then a week gets busy, neither of you brings it up, and the whole thing dissolves without anybody deciding to stop.


That is not a willpower problem. It is usually a design problem. The check-in you set up was too long, too vague, or too risky to attempt on a Tuesday when you are both tired.


## Why the Sunday-night version dies by week three


The standard advice is to block out an hour, put the phones away, and talk about the relationship. It sounds right. It rarely survives contact with a real month.


- **An hour is a commitment, and commitments get postponed.** Twenty minutes is harder to talk yourself out of. So is a walk.
- **"How are we doing?" is not an agenda.** It sounds generous and lands as an interrogation. The more anxious person gets a stage. The more avoidant one has nowhere to stand.
- **The last one went badly.** One honest sentence turned into[the same argument you have been having for years](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-keep-having-the-same-argument) , and now the ritual itself feels like a trapdoor.
- **It quietly became admin.** You sat down to talk about the two of you and spent the time on the calendar, the car, and who is calling the plumber. This is how couples[turn into a logistics team](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/weve-become-a-logistics-team-not-a-couple) without noticing.


## A check-in is not a performance review


The distinction matters more than any list of questions.


A performance review is retrospective and evaluative. Someone has prepared. Someone is being assessed. The person on the receiving end spends the whole thing waiting to find out how badly they did, which means they are defending rather than listening.


A check-in is closer to maintenance. You are not grading each other. You are looking for the small thing that is starting to catch, before it becomes the thing you argue about at midnight. Most of a good check-in should be boring. If yours are consistently dramatic, you are not doing check-ins, you are doing crisis meetings on a schedule.


## The part people miss: the problem had a date on it


Here is something that shows up constantly on the Maia side, and it is not what people expect.


When someone brings a serious problem to Maia, one of the first things they do is date it. Not "we have always been like this," but "it started around the time he changed jobs" or "it has been like this since we moved." They can name the season it began. Sometimes the week.


Which means the thing was legible long before it became a crisis. It was visible to at least one person, for months, and it never got said out loud, because on any particular ordinary evening it did not feel big enough to raise. Not worth a whole conversation. Not worth the risk of ruining a decent night.


That is what a check-in is actually for. Not to fix anything. To lower the bar for what counts as worth mentioning, so that the small version gets said while it is still small. Couples who[let things build up](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-avoid-hard-conversations) are almost never avoiding a big problem. They are deferring a series of tiny ones.


## What an AI read adds that the ritual alone does not


You can do a perfectly good check-in with nothing but a kitchen table. Plenty of couples do.


Where it helps to have something neutral in the room is with the part neither of you can see from inside it. You are both unreliable narrators of your own conversations, not because you are lying, but because you remember the sentence that stung and forget the twenty around it.


If you record a check-in together with **Heal Together** , Maia gives you both a shared read of it afterward. What surprises people is almost never the content. It is the proportions: how much of the twenty minutes went to one topic, who introduced every subject, how often one person started a sentence and then abandoned it.[The things an outside listener catches in a conversation](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/what-ai-hears-in-your-arguments) tend to be structural rather than emotional, and structure is exactly what you cannot track while you are busy having feelings.


**Reflect with Maia** is the solo version. Useful when you are the one who can tell something is off but cannot name it yet, and going in with "I don't know, something feels wrong" would put your partner on the defensive for no reason. Getting clear first is not going behind their back. It is showing up with a sentence instead of a mood.


## Making one that survives a busy month


The check-ins that last tend to share a few features. Steal what is useful.


- **Attach it to something you already do.** Sunday groceries, the drive back from her parents', the twenty minutes after the kids are down. Rituals that require a new slot in the calendar lose to the calendar.
- **Keep it short enough to be unimpressive.** Fifteen or twenty minutes. The goal is frequency, not depth. Depth is what happens when frequency has made it safe.
- **Use narrow questions, not open ones.** "What was the best part of your week and what was the worst?" beats "how are we doing?" So does "was there a moment this week I got something wrong and you let it go?" That last one is uncomfortable and it is the most useful question on this page.
- **Include something good on purpose.** Name one thing they did that you noticed. Not as a sweetener before the criticism. Most people are running a deficit on being noticed, and the check-in is where you pay it down.
- **End with one concrete thing, or nothing.** "We'll do Thursday night without screens" is a check-in. "We'll communicate better" is a feeling that dressed up as a plan.
- **Let it be allowed to be fine.** A check-in where you both say things are good and then talk about something else is a successful check-in. It is not a waste of a slot.


## The version of this that backfires


Two failure modes worth naming.


The first is using the check-in as a delivery mechanism for grievances you have been stockpiling. If your partner learns that the ritual is where they get handed the invoice, they will find reasons to be busy, and they will be right to.


The second is treating a check-in as a substitute for saying things in the moment. "I'll bring it up Sunday" is a reasonable thought once. As a habit it turns you into your own bottleneck, and the thing arrives on Sunday with four days of interest on it. The point of the ritual is to make small mentions easier everywhere, not to funnel everything into one appointment.


And if you keep doing them and nothing changes, at some point the honest reading is that the format is not the obstacle. A check-in only works between two people who both want to know the answer. If one of you is attending to prove they attended, that is its own conversation, and it is a bigger one than[any habit you could build together](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/how-to-have-a-healthy-relationship-5-tips-that-work-for-everyone) .


If you are trying to work out what your own check-in should even cover, or you have a sense that something has been off for a while and you cannot get it into words, that is a good thing to talk through with Maia. Alone first, if that is easier, or together when you are ready. Most of what gets brought to Maia started as something someone almost mentioned months earlier and did not.
